name: Spatial Frequency Distribution Map
description: Maps local spatial frequency distributions — AI-generated content shows abnormal frequency energy distributions across regions.
mechanism:
This method maps the spatial distribution of frequency energy across the image to detect AI-generated content and localize manipulation:

1. **Local Power Spectrum Computation**: The image is divided into overlapping blocks of size N×N (typically 64×64). For each block, the 2D DFT is computed and the azimuthally-averaged power spectrum P(f) is obtained by averaging |F(u,v)|² over all frequency components at radial frequency f = √(u² + v²). In natural images, P(f) follows a power law P(f) ∝ 1/f^α with exponent α ≈ 2.0 ± 0.5 (Field, 1987). The local spectral exponent α is estimated by linear regression of log P vs log f.

2. **Spectral Exponent Map**: The local α values are assembled into a spatial map. In authentic photographs, α varies smoothly: textured regions have lower α (≈ 1.5, flatter spectrum with more high-frequency content) while smooth regions have higher α (≈ 2.5, steeper spectrum dominated by low frequencies). AI-generated images often show: (a) more uniform α across the image, (b) different α ranges than natural images (particularly at high frequencies), and (c) abrupt α transitions not aligned with content boundaries.

3. **Band-Limited Energy Ratio Analysis**: The frequency spectrum is divided into bands: low (0–f_N/8), mid (f_N/8–f_N/4), and high (f_N/4–f_N/2), where f_N is the Nyquist frequency. The energy ratios R_LM = E_low/E_mid and R_MH = E_mid/E_high are computed per block. Natural photographs maintain characteristic ratios determined by scene content and camera optics. GAN-generated images often show energy deficits at the highest frequencies (high R_MH), while diffusion model outputs may show more natural spectra but with subtle band-specific anomalies.

4. **Inter-Region Spectral Consistency**: For manipulation detection, the method compares the spectral characteristics of different image regions. In an unmanipulated photograph, all regions share the same optical transfer function (same lens, same focus distance for in-focus areas). The method detects spectral inconsistencies by computing the Jensen-Shannon divergence between normalized power spectra of different blocks. Blocks with divergence > threshold from their neighbors indicate potential splicing or AI inpainting.
parameters:
Block size: 64×64 pixels
Block overlap: 50%
Frequency bands: low [0, f_N/8], mid [f_N/8, f_N/4], high [f_N/4, f_N/2]
Spectral exponent: α = slope of log P(f) vs log f
Expected natural α range: 1.5–2.5
JS divergence threshold: > 0.15
Minimum image size: 128×128 pixels
accuracy: 79–87% accuracy for AI-generated image detection via spectral exponent analysis. Band-limited energy ratio achieves AUC of 0.88 for GAN detection. Spectral consistency for splicing detection: F1-score of 0.82. α-map analysis is particularly effective on StyleGAN (87%) and ProGAN (85%) but less effective on diffusion models (76%).
source: Field, D. J. (1987). Relations between the Statistics of Natural Images and the Response Properties of Cortical Cells. Journal of the Optical Society of America A, 4(12), 2379–2394.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated images through abnormal spatial frequency distributions. Identifying GAN outputs from high-frequency energy deficiency. Localizing spliced or inpainted regions through spectral inconsistency. Characterizing image processing history from frequency domain signatures.
strengths:
• 1/f power law is a fundamental property of natural images — well-established theory
• Spectral exponent provides a compact, interpretable feature per region
• Band-limited energy ratios target known GAN spectral deficiencies
• Inter-region consistency analysis localizes manipulated regions
• Computationally efficient with FFT-based implementation
limitations:
• Modern diffusion models produce more natural spectral distributions than GANs
• JPEG compression alters the high-frequency spectrum, reducing discriminative power
• Highly textured or uniform images produce extreme α values naturally
• Image resizing changes the spectral profile, requiring careful normalization
• Scene-dependent α variation complicates global thresholding
